human_tolerance.notes: Urbanity is region-dependent, so this is an Adapter rather than an Exploiter: the tree sparrow is 'widespread in the towns and cities of eastern Asia' and is the most common city bird in the Philippines, but in Europe 'it inhabits lightly wooded open countryside, while the house sparrow breeds in more urban areas', and it is 'a rural bird in Europe, but an urban bird in eastern Asia'. In its introduced North American range it competes poorly with the house sparrow in urban centres and is therefore mainly found in parks, farms and rural woods. It is markedly warier than the house sparrow: captive birds showed 'lower willingness to eat novel foods and habituated more slowly to novel objects'. It visits feeding stations, especially for peanuts.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Wikipedia gives no month-level breeding calendar for any region, only that two or three broods may be raised each year, with 12-13 days of incubation and a further 15-18 days to fledging, and that the male proclaims nest ownership in spring and repeats the display in autumn. The start and end dates are a judgement spanning spring and summer for the East Asian target regions, not a sourced window.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: 'In winter, seed resources are most likely to be a key limiting factor. At this time of year, individuals in a flock establish linear dominance hierarchies.' The exact boundary dates are a judgement.

vocalizations.description: Excited series of tschip calls, given by unpaired or courting males calling from near the nest site to proclaim ownership and attract a mate. Recorded as a Chirp rather than a Song because the species has no true song; this call fills the behaviour program's song slot.
Monosyllabic chirps used for social interaction between birds in a flock.

Harsh monosyllabic flight call, given by birds flushing from a feeding flock. Wikipedia describes it as the flight call rather than an alarm call, so it is bound to the behaviour program's alarm slot as the harshest and most threat-adjacent call the species has.

taxonomy.note: The GBIF species match on Passer montanus returns usageKey 5231198, rank SPECIES, status ACCEPTED, order Passeriformes, family Passeridae, genus Passer. The ITIS JSON service returns Passer montanus, TSN 179630, author (Linnaeus, 1758).

external.note: gbif_usage_key 5231198 from the GBIF species match API; inat_taxon_id 13851 from the iNaturalist taxa API (active, rank species, preferred common name 'Eurasian Tree Sparrow'); wikidata Q25968 taken from the English Wikipedia page's wikibase item; itis_tsn 179630 from the ITIS JSON service by scientific name. Wikidata's own P846 on this item holds 5231198, the GBIF key rather than an ITIS TSN, so the TSN is taken from ITIS directly.

common_names.note: en from the iNaturalist preferred common name and the English article title; fr (Moineau friquet), de (Feldsperling), nl (Ringmus), ja (スズメ), ko (참새) and zh (麻雀) from the Wikidata sitelink titles of the same item. The German, Dutch and Hungarian names are regional: Wikipedia notes that the German Feldsperling and the Hungarian mezei veréb ('field sparrow') describe its open-country habit better than the English name does.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 on Q25968 is Q211005 (least concern). Wikipedia: 'the species' conservation status is evaluated at the global level as being of Least Concern', with an estimated population of 190-310 million individuals and an estimated range of 98.3 million square kilometres.

range.note: Country lists derived from the range, distribution and subspecies sections. Native: the general statement is 'most of temperate Europe and Asia south of about latitude 68 degrees N ... and through Southeast Asia to Java and Bali'. P. m. montanus covers Europe except 'the southwestern Iberian Peninsula, southern Greece and the former Yugoslavia', and Asia east to the Lena River and south to northern Turkey, the Caucasus, Kazakhstan, Mongolia and North Korea; transcaucasicus the southern Caucasus east to northern Iran; dilutus extreme northeastern Iran, northern Pakistan and northwestern India, plus Uzbekistan and Tajikistan east to China; tibetanus Nepal east through Tibet to northwestern China; saturatus Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea; malaccensis the southern Himalayas east to Hainan and Indonesia; hepaticus northeastern Assam to northwestern Burma. GR is omitted because southern Greece is explicitly excepted, and FO, MT and GO are omitted because the article says the species 'formerly bred in the Faroes, Malta and Gozo', which is extirpation rather than native range. Introduced: 'introduced successfully to Sardinia, eastern Indonesia, the Philippines and Micronesia'; ship-carried birds that 'colonised Borneo' (MY); the established population of about 15,000 birds around St. Louis descended from 20 imported from Germany and released in 1870 (US); and presence in Melbourne, towns in central and northern Victoria and the Riverina region of New South Wales (AU). NZ and BM are omitted because 'introductions to New Zealand and Bermuda did not take root'. Sardinia sits inside the native IT and eastern Indonesia inside the native ID, which country codes cannot express. Occasional vagrants (Gibraltar, Tunisia, Algeria, Egypt, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Iceland) are not listed as range. Koppen classes are a judgement from the described range: Cfb for temperate oceanic western Europe; Cfa and Cwa for humid subtropical and monsoon-influenced eastern China, Korea and southern Japan; Csa for the Mediterranean part of the European range; Dfa, Dfb and Dfc for the Manchurian, Siberian continental and subarctic belt below 68 degrees N; BSh for the Caspian, Central Asian and Iranian steppe; and Am for Java and Bali.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Hop is a judgement: the article describes the genus as 'primarily ground-feeding seed-eaters' and this species as feeding 'on the ground in flocks', and BirdFuncDat gives ForStrat-ground 33, but neither source states that it hops rather than walks. Hop is therefore carried over from the congener house sparrow record, where Wikipedia does state it. Fly follows from flight: Powered. Swimming is not described for this species and is omitted.

traits.thermoregulation.note: The article's temperature regulation section describes increased body mass and basal metabolic rate, cytochrome c oxidase activity and thyroid hormone levels in response to cold, all endothermic responses.

traits.perching.note: A perching passerine that is 'often depicted either perched on a plant spray or flying in a flock' in art, roosts in trees, and uses pollarded willows and gorse as nest sites.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The untidy nest of the tree sparrow is built in a natural cavity, a hole in a building, or the disused nest of a European magpie or white stork', and it 'typically builds its nest in a cavity in an old tree or rock face'. The common name is 'given because it prefers tree holes for nesting'.

traits.mass_kg.note: 'The tree sparrow is 12.5-14 cm long, with a wingspan of about 21 cm and a weight of 24 g'. The BirdFuncDat row gives BodyMass-Value 21.39 g (Dunning08), slightly lighter, so mass_kg uses the article's stated 24 g. The article gives no mass range, so mass_range_kg is omitted rather than invented.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of '12.5-14 cm long', which is 0.125-0.14 m.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The maximum recorded age is 13.1 years, but three years is a typical lifespan.'

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-Seed 60, Diet-Inv 40, Diet-PlantO 0, Diet-Fruit 0, Diet-5Cat PlantSeed, Diet-Certainty A, from the BirdFuncDat row for Passer montanus. Wikipedia agrees: 'a bird that predominantly eats seeds and grains', a diet including 'weed seeds, such as chickweeds and goosefoot, spilled grain', and invertebrates 'such as insects, woodlice, millipedes, centipedes, spiders and harvestmen' when the young are 'fed mainly on animal food'.

traits.social.note: 'It feeds on the ground in flocks, often alongside house sparrows, finches, or buntings', and 'individuals in a flock establish linear dominance hierarchies', so Flock. Wikipedia also records that pairs 'may breed in isolation or loose colonies'. group_size is a judgement: no flock size is given, so the congener house sparrow's range is carried across.

traits.activity_pattern.note: EltonTraits Nocturnal 0. Wikipedia describes daytime ground feeding in flocks and communal winter roosting.

traits.defense.note: 'The risk of predation affects feeding strategies. One study showed that when the distance between shelter and food sources increased, birds visited feeders in smaller flocks, spent less time there, and became more vigilant when far from shelter.' Predators listed include the Eurasian sparrowhawk, common kestrel and little owl, and nests are raided by magpies, jays, least weasels, rats and cats.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement, set well above the house sparrow's value because of the documented neophobia: 'one factor limiting the spread of tree sparrows in North America is the species' higher neophobia (novelty aversion) compared to house sparrows; one study specifically found that captive tree sparrows showed lower willingness to eat novel foods and habituated more slowly to novel objects than house sparrows', and because in Europe it is a countryside bird that 'avoids breeding on intensively managed mixed farmland'.

habitat.use.note: ForStrat-ground 33, ForStrat-understory 33, ForStrat-midhigh 33, from the BirdFuncDat row for Passer montanus. The schema has no mid-storey stratum, so understory and midhigh are both mapped to arboreal, giving ground 0.33 and arboreal 0.66.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Nests in cavities in old trees, rock faces and building holes, and among the roots of gorse and similar bushes.

habitat.resources.note: Seed and invertebrate weights follow the EltonTraits diet shares (60/40). Cavity nesting is weight 1.0 because the species is a cavity nester that 'will readily use nest boxes' but 'shows a strong preference for nest-sites near wetland habitats'. Perch and shrub_thicket shelter weights are judgement: the article describes 'pollarded willows along slow water courses', 'open countryside with small isolated patches of woodland', and nests 'among roots of overhanging gorse or similar bushes'.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity is derived from the explicit Europe and east-Asia contrast: 'The tree sparrow is widespread in the towns and cities of eastern Asia, but in Europe, it inhabits lightly wooded open countryside, while the house sparrow breeds in more urban areas', and 'The tree sparrow is a rural bird in Europe, but is an urban bird in eastern Asia'. Adapter rather than Exploiter because in the introduced North American range it 'has to compete with the house sparrow in urban centres, and is therefore mainly found in parks, farms and rural woods'. uses_gardens follows those passages plus 'it may also visit feeding stations, especially for peanuts'. road_mortality is High from 'The house sparrow and tree sparrow are the most frequent victims of roadkill on the roads of Central, Eastern and Southern Europe'. light_max is a judgement: unlike the house sparrow, no night feeding under artificial light is reported, and winter foraging is described as daytime flock feeding.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'It is sedentary over most of its extensive range, but northernmost breeding populations migrate south for the winter, and small numbers leave southern Europe for North Africa and the Middle East.' Resident over most of a range covering all four target regions, so ActiveYearRound rather than Migration.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding and winter flocking are both described, but without a month-level calendar for any region, so the phase boundaries are judgement. Supporting detail: 'Two or three broods may be raised each year'; the male 'calls from near the nest site to proclaim ownership and attract a mate' in spring and 'These behaviours are repeated in autumn'; and the winter flock dominance-hierarchy description. The phases carry no region code because the dates are not region-specific.

seasonal.life_stages.note: duration_days 31 is the upper bound of the sourced pre-fledging period: 'The eggs are incubated by both parents for 12-13 days' and 'A further 15-18 days elapse before they fledge', giving 27-31 days from laying to fledging. The bird 'reaches breeding maturity within a year of hatching', so no separate subadult stage is added. scale 0.85 is a judgement for a small passerine juvenile and is not a sourced figure.

vocalizations.tschip.note: 'The tree sparrow does not have a true song, but its vocalisations include an excited series of tschip calls made by unpaired or courting males.' Recorded with context Chirp rather than Song to reflect that the species has no true song, and bound to the behaviour program's song slot because it is the courtship and nest-ownership display. The article gives no time of day for the display; DawnChorus and Dusk are included because the shared program only sings at low sun angles, and the call is described as 'excited', which is consistent with a display at either end of the day.

vocalizations.chirp.note: 'Other monosyllabic chirps are used for social interaction.'

vocalizations.teck.note: 'the flight call is a harsh teck.' The article calls this the flight call, not an alarm call, so the context is a judgement: the program requires an alarm call, and this is the harshest, most threat-adjacent call the species has, being given on flushing.

look.note: Plumage from the Description section: 'The adult's crown and nape are rich chestnut, and there is a kidney-shaped black ear patch on each pure white cheek; the chin, throat, and the area between the bill and throat are black. The upperparts are light brown, streaked with black, and the brown wings have two distinct narrow white bars. The legs are pale brown, and the bill is lead-blue in summer, becoming almost black in winter.' The sexes are alike, so no sexual dimorphism is modelled. Modelled features: the crown and nape boxes carry the rich chestnut (markings); the head base and breast use the near-white belly slot, giving the pure white cheek; the mirrored cheek box is the black ear patch; and the bib box is the black chin and throat. The bill is mapped to the near-black eye slot for the dark lead-blue to almost-black bill. The two white wing bars, the black streaking on the upperparts and the black streaking on the crown are not modelled: a box thin enough to read as a bar sat inside the wing, and a box thick enough to clear it read as a plank through the wing in the previewer. Proportions are judgement, mostly carried from the congener house sparrow record, with tail_ratio and beak_ratio shortened for the genus's 'short square tails and stubby conical beaks'.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program. food_tag seed follows the EltonTraits and Wikipedia diet. song is bound to the courtship tschip and alarm to the harsh flight teck because the species has no true song; both are calls the program needs and both are described. flee_m 5 reflects a species with higher neophobia than the house sparrow. nest_m1 3 and nest_m2 8 bracket two or three broods a year and must include months 4 and 5, which the program hardcodes.
